series.name: ₹100 Crore Startup
series.tagline: A startup that crashed. Told in reverse. Every episode goes back one step.
series.concept: Episode 1 opens with the company dead. Each episode rewinds time, revealing what went wrong. The audience watches a success story unravel backwards — seeing the red flags the founder missed. Every episode ends with 'But 3 months earlier...' pulling viewers to the next episode.

episodes.title: The Crash

slides.text: January 15, 2026. QuickKart's servers went offline at 3:42 PM. 400 employees found out they were jobless from a LinkedIn post. Not even an email. A LinkedIn post.
Arjun Kapoor. 28. IIT Bombay. McKinsey for 2 years. Left to build QuickKart — a 10-minute grocery delivery app. Raised ₹100 crore in 18 months. Lost all of it in 6.
₹100 crore raised. ₹47 crore on marketing. ₹28 crore on dark stores that never hit capacity. ₹15 crore on 'team building' and a Goa offsite. ₹10 crore they still can't account for.

Three lawsuits. Investors wanted their money back. Vendors hadn't been paid in four months. And one employee had filed an FIR. Arjun's lawyer said two words: 'Settle everything.' He couldn't. There was no money left.

How does a company that raised ₹100 crore die in 6 months? Was it bad luck? Bad decisions? Or was it designed to fail from the start? The answer isn't in what went wrong. It's in what went right — too fast.

episodes.synopsis: Day zero. The startup is dead. ₹100 crore in losses. The founder sits alone in an empty office.
episodes.caption: ₹100 crore. 400 jobs. Gone in 6 months. This is the story of QuickKart — told in reverse. Every episode goes back one step. What would YOU have done differently? 💸

episodes.title: The Best Month

slides.text: July 2025. QuickKart crossed ₹8 crore monthly revenue. Arjun rented out a Bandra rooftop. Open bar. DJ. The investors were thrilled. The board sent champagne. What nobody mentioned — the cost to earn that ₹8 crore was ₹14 crore.

Every order cost QuickKart ₹340 to deliver. The average order value? ₹220. They lost ₹120 on EVERY single order. Arjun's answer: 'We'll fix unit economics at scale.' It's the most expensive sentence in startup history.

More orders = more losses. But more orders also meant better metrics to show investors. Arjun was trapped. Stop growing = investors panic. Keep growing = burn cash faster. He chose growth. Every failing startup does.
One person saw it. Neha — the CFO. She sent a 12-page report to Arjun: 'At current burn rate, we have 8 months of runway.' Arjun read it. Thanked her. Did nothing. The report gathered dust.

The best month was the beginning of the end. Revenue was a vanity metric. The real number — cash in bank — was dropping ₹6 crore every month. But 3 months earlier, something happened that made the burn rate explode.

episodes.synopsis: Six months before the crash. QuickKart just had its highest revenue month. Everyone was celebrating. Nobody saw the cracks.
episodes.caption: ₹8 crore revenue. ₹14 crore cost. Losing money on EVERY order and celebrating. The CFO warned them. Nobody listened. What happened 3 months before that made things worse? 📉

episodes.title: The Deal

slides.text: FlashBasket. Same model — 10-minute grocery. Better funded. Backed by SoftPay Ventures. They were killing QuickKart in South Mumbai. Arjun had two choices: fight or deal.

They met at a Bandra hotel. Arjun, his lawyer, and FlashBasket's CEO — Vikram Joshi. Smooth. Calm. Yale MBA. He proposed: 'You take the suburbs. We take South Mumbai. No competition. Both grow.' It sounded perfect.

Page 47. Clause 12.3(b). 'If either party's monthly active users drop below 100,000, the territory agreement is void and the other party gains exclusive access to both territories.' Arjun's lawyer flagged it. Arjun overruled him. 'Our MAU is 3 lakhs. We'll never drop that low.'

Within 3 months, QuickKart's suburbs-only strategy backfired. Suburban customers had lower order frequency. MAU dropped to 2.8 lakh, then 2.1. Meanwhile, FlashBasket launched aggressive discounting in South Mumbai. Their MAU soared.

The deal that was supposed to save QuickKart had a kill switch built in. And Vikram knew it. He'd designed it. But 2 months before the deal, something else happened — the hire that started the real damage.

episodes.synopsis: April 2025. Arjun made a deal with competitor FlashBasket to split territories. The deal had a clause nobody read carefully.
episodes.caption: A territory deal with a hidden kill switch. The competitor designed it to win. And Arjun signed it without reading page 47. Have you ever signed something without reading the fine print? 📝

episodes.title: The Hire

slides.text: Rohit Malhotra. Ex-Amazon. Ex-Flipkart. MBA from ISB. His resume was a startup founder's dream. His salary demand — ₹85 lakhs per year. Arjun didn't negotiate. First mistake.

Rohit's growth strategy: spend. ₹10 crore on influencer marketing. ₹5 crore on cricket sponsorship. ₹3 crore on a Bollywood brand ambassador. 'You have to spend money to make money,' he said. He was half right.
Neha ran the numbers. The influencer campaigns had a 0.3% conversion rate. They were paying ₹2,000 to acquire each customer. Each customer ordered twice and never came back. The math was murder.
What Arjun didn't know: Rohit's 'ex-Amazon' stint was 11 months. He was let go. His 'ex-Flipkart' role was a contract position. The references Arjun never called would have said one word: avoid.

Rohit burned ₹18 crore in 3 months. The growth he delivered was a mirage — users who came for discounts and vanished. But the hire wasn't the real origin. 4 months before Rohit, the fundraising round happened. And that's where the real poison entered.

episodes.synopsis: February 2025. Arjun hires Rohit Malhotra as VP of Growth. Impressive resume. Expensive salary. Terrible intentions.
episodes.caption: ₹85 lakh salary. ₹18 crore burned. Zero reference checks. The VP of Growth who accelerated the death. Have you ever trusted a resume without checking? 📋

episodes.title: The Money

slides.text: Arjun pitched 43 investors. 41 said no. Two said yes — NexGen Capital and SilkRoute Fund. Together: ₹100 crore for 30% equity. Arjun cried in his car after signing. Happy tears. They wouldn't stay happy.

The money came with conditions. Board seats for both investors. A mandatory spend of ₹40 crore on growth in the first 6 months. And a 'ratchet clause' — if QuickKart didn't hit ₹500 crore valuation by Series B, Arjun's stake would get diluted to 8%.
₹40 crore mandatory spend meant Arjun HAD to burn cash fast. He couldn't be frugal even if he wanted to. The investors designed it this way — spend fast, grow fast, raise again. Or lose your company.

NexGen wanted quick returns — flip the investment in 18 months. SilkRoute wanted market dominance — burn cash until competitors die. Two investors. Two opposite strategies. One founder caught between them.

The money was both the fuel and the fire. It forced bad hires, bad deals, bad spending. But before the money — there was the idea. And the idea had a flaw that nobody, not even Arjun, had questioned. 6 months before the raise, the flaw was already visible.

episodes.synopsis: October 2024. The Series A round closes. ₹100 crore from two firms. The term sheet has conditions that will haunt Arjun.
episodes.caption: ₹100 crore with strings that guaranteed bad decisions. Mandatory spending. Ratchet clauses. Two investors with opposite goals. The money was the weapon. Who designed it to be? 💰

episodes.title: The Flaw

slides.text: 10-minute delivery needs dark stores every 2 km. In Mumbai, that's 65 dark stores minimum. Rent alone: ₹1.3 crore per month. Before a single order. Before a single delivery person. Just rent.

Neha — before she was CFO, she was QuickKart's first financial analyst. She wrote a model in April 2024. 'This business needs ₹200 crore to reach profitability. And that's the optimistic scenario.' Arjun read it. He changed the assumptions.

'Every great company loses money in the beginning,' Arjun told himself. Amazon lost money for 7 years. Uber is still losing. But here's the thing — Amazon had AWS. Uber has global scale. QuickKart had... vibes.

Arjun rewrote the pitch deck. The ₹200 crore problem became a '₹60 crore path to profitability.' He showed investors a different model. The one Neha built stayed buried in a folder called 'Old Versions.' It was 6 months old.

Arjun didn't lie to investors. He lied to himself first. But the lie needed one more person to become real — a co-founder who believed it. And 3 months before the model was built, that co-founder walked away.

episodes.synopsis: April 2024. QuickKart's core model has a fundamental problem — the 10-minute promise is only possible at a loss. Arjun knows. He buries it.
episodes.caption: He knew the model was broken. He changed the numbers instead of the model. Every startup that fails has a moment where the founder chose comfortable lies over uncomfortable truths. When was yours? 📊

episodes.title: The Co-Founder

slides.text: Priya Sharma. Co-founder. CTO. The one who actually built QuickKart's tech. While Arjun pitched, she coded. While he networked, she solved logistics. They were the perfect team. Until they weren't.

'We should be a 30-minute delivery service,' Priya said. 'The math works at 30 minutes. We can be profitable in 2 years.' Arjun laughed. 'Nobody's funding a 30-minute app. 10 minutes is the story that raises money.'

The real fight happened over Arjun's new pitch deck. Priya saw the changed numbers. 'You edited my financial model? You showed investors made-up projections?' Arjun said, 'Aspirational projections.' She said, 'That's called fraud.'

Priya resigned. No drama. No LinkedIn rant. She sent a one-line email: 'I can't build something I don't believe in. Wish you the best.' She walked out at 6 PM on a Tuesday. The building didn't notice.

With Priya gone, there was nobody to question Arjun. Nobody to say 'that math doesn't work.' Nobody to call his bluff. The company became a one-man show. And one-man shows always end the same way. But 8 months before Priya left, they were still friends. Still dreaming on a Juhu beach.

episodes.synopsis: January 2024. Priya Sharma, the co-founder and CTO, quits. The reason — she saw what Arjun was becoming.
episodes.caption: The co-founder who built the product left. The one who sold the dream stayed. And without her, there was no one to say "stop." Who's your Priya? The person whose exit you'd never recover from? 🚪

episodes.title: The Beach

slides.text: May 2023. Juhu beach. Arjun ordered groceries on Blinkit. Estimated delivery: 18 minutes. Actual delivery: 47 minutes. His ice cream melted. 'I could build something faster,' he said. Priya laughed. 'Prove it.'

They drew the first map in the sand. Dark stores close to customers. Optimized routes. AI-powered inventory prediction. Priya solved the tech. Arjun solved the story. By sunset, QuickKart existed — in sand.

They made each other a promise that night. 'We build something real. Not a hype machine. If the math doesn't work, we pivot. If it can't be profitable, we stop. Deal.' They shook on it. Both meant it.
Next 6 months — the best of their lives. Priya built the app from scratch. Arjun pitched 15 angel investors, got 8. First dark store in Andheri. First delivery — 9 minutes and 12 seconds. They cried.

This was the moment QuickKart was pure. Before the investors, before the VP of Growth, before the lies. Just two friends and a better mousetrap. But every startup origin story has something it doesn't show — the ambition that'll turn toxic. Arjun's was already whispering.

episodes.synopsis: May 2023. The origin story. Two friends on Juhu beach, complaining about grocery delivery, sketching a company in the sand.
episodes.caption: Every startup starts with a pure moment. Two friends, one problem, an honest promise. What happened between the beach and the crash wasn't bad luck. It was choices. One at a time. Each one making the next one easier. 🏖️

episodes.title: The Aftermath — Arjun

slides.text: After QuickKart died, Arjun disappeared. Deleted Instagram. Changed his number. Moved back to his parents' house in Lucknow. For three months, he didn't leave his room.
The lawsuits settled for ₹4.2 crore — paid by insurance and asset liquidation. But the personal guarantee on the office lease? ₹78 lakhs. From Arjun's pocket. A pocket that was empty.

Month four. Neha called. The CFO who warned him about everything. She didn't say 'I told you so.' She said, 'I'm starting a financial consulting firm for startups. I need a partner who's failed at everything. You're perfect.'

Their first client? A 10-minute delivery startup. Arjun looked at their pitch deck and saw himself — same lies, same inflated model, same ignored math. He told them the truth. They fired him. Then hired him back a month later when their CFO quit.

Arjun's consulting firm doesn't have a fancy office. It has a rule on the wall: 'If the math doesn't work, change the model, not the math.' Neha's words. The words he should have listened to from day one.

episodes.synopsis: Post-crash. What happened to founder Arjun. The lawsuits, the depression, and an unexpected restart.
episodes.caption: He failed with ₹100 crore. He's rebuilding with honesty. Sometimes the best startup lesson costs everything. What would you do after losing it all? 🔄

episodes.title: The 400

slides.text: 400 employees. Most found out at 3:42 PM on a Wednesday. By 4 PM, 'QuickKart' was trending. By 5 PM, LinkedIn was flooded with 'open to work' badges. By 6 PM, rival companies were sending DMs. Vultures and lifelines look the same.

178 delivery riders. Not on payroll — 'gig partners.' No severance. No notice. Most had EMIs on their bikes. QuickKart's Instagram still had a post celebrating 'our amazing delivery fleet' — posted three days before shutting them out.

The tech team had it slightly better — engineers get hired fast. But 23 of them had joined in the last 3 months. They'd left stable jobs at TCS, Infosys, Wipro for 'the startup dream.' Three months of salary. Three months of dream. Both gone.
47 dark stores. The perishable inventory? Dumped. Thousands of kilos of fruits, vegetables, dairy — all wasted. A grocery delivery company ended by throwing away groceries. The irony writes itself.

₹100 crore didn't just evaporate. It became other people's problems. EMIs, broken leases, wasted food, lost careers. A founder's ambition is a bet — but the chips are other people's lives. That's the part the pitch deck never shows.

episodes.synopsis: The employees who lost their jobs overnight. Their stories. Their survival. The human cost of a startup's ego.
episodes.caption: 400 lives disrupted. 178 riders with no severance. Food dumped while delivery riders couldn't afford dinner. The pitch deck never has a slide for this. Should it? 🧑‍🤝‍🧑

episodes.title: The One Who Left

slides.text: Priya didn't start another startup immediately. She took 6 months off. Traveled to Kerala. Read books. Didn't open LinkedIn once. When people asked 'what are you doing,' she said 'nothing.' It was the most productive nothing of her life.

In the silence, she figured it out. The 10-minute delivery problem wasn't about speed. It was about inventory prediction. If you stock the RIGHT items within 5 km of the RIGHT people, delivery time drops naturally.
She built StockSense — not a delivery app but an AI inventory tool for kirana stores. Tells them what to stock based on their neighborhood's patterns. No dark stores. No delivery fleet. Just math.

StockSense has 4,000 kirana store subscribers. ₹500/month per store. Revenue: ₹2 crore/year. Profit: ₹85 lakhs. No investors. No boards. No Goa offsites. Just a profitable company built on the math Arjun didn't want to hear.

When QuickKart crashed, a reporter called Priya for comment. She said, 'I'm sorry for the 400 people. The idea wasn't wrong. The ambition was.' She hung up. Went back to her spreadsheet. The math still worked.

episodes.synopsis: Priya's story after leaving QuickKart. She built something quieter. Something that worked.
episodes.caption: She left the ₹100 crore rocket. Built a ₹2 crore steady ship. No fame, no headlines, no Forbes list. Just profit. Was Priya the real winner all along? 🛶

episodes.title: The Competitor

slides.text: Vikram Joshi didn't want to beat QuickKart. He wanted to buy it. For cheap. The territory deal was step one — weaken them. The clause was step two — trigger the kill switch. Step three? Buy the corpse.
Two weeks after QuickKart shut down, FlashBasket offered to buy the brand, tech, and customer database. For ₹3 crore. A ₹100 crore company sold for the price of a South Mumbai apartment.

FlashBasket didn't want QuickKart's brand. They wanted the dark store leases — 47 locations already built out. And the customer data — 3 lakh users with purchasing history. They paid ₹3 crore for what cost ₹50 crore to build.
This wasn't Vikram's first kill. Before QuickKart — DashMart (₹2 crore buyout), InstaGrocer (₹1.5 crore), FreshRun (₹4 crore). Four competitors. Four kills. Same playbook every time.

Vikram's strategy worked because founders are desperate to believe someone wants to play fair. Nobody reads page 47. Nobody checks the pattern. The best predator doesn't look like one. But karma moves slower than ambition. And it was coming.

episodes.synopsis: Vikram Joshi and FlashBasket. The territory deal wasn't chance. It was a calculated acquisition strategy.
episodes.caption: Four companies killed with the same playbook. Territory deal, kill clause, buy the corpse. Nobody read page 47. What would Vikram's page 47 look like? 🕸️

episodes.title: The Karma

slides.text: FlashBasket now had 180 dark stores across Mumbai. 12 lakh users. ₹500 crore valuation. Vikram was on every podcast. Every panel. 'The king of quick commerce.' But kings need revenue, not just territory.

Four acquired companies. Four different tech stacks. Four different supplier contracts. Merging them was supposed to take 3 months. It took 11. And during those 11 months, customers experienced the worst service of their lives.

SoftPay Ventures — FlashBasket's lead investor — sent a team to audit. The findings: 40% of claimed 'active users' hadn't ordered in 3 months. The dark stores from acquisitions were running at 30% capacity. The ₹500 crore valuation was fiction.

Vikram's playbook killed competitors but created a bloated monster. He was brilliant at destroying but terrible at building. The exact opposite of Arjun's problem. Two founders. Two mirror-image failures.

SoftPay gave Vikram an ultimatum: find a Series C investor in 90 days or they pull funding. Vikram needed a miracle. And then Priya's StockSense data showed up on his radar. A small company with the one thing he didn't have — a product that actually worked.

episodes.synopsis: FlashBasket's own cracks start showing. Vikram's strategy of buying competitors worked — until the acquisitions had to actually perform.
episodes.caption: The company killer's own company is dying. And the only thing that can save it was built by the woman he indirectly destroyed. Karma doesn't need to be fast. It just needs to be accurate. 🎯

episodes.title: The Call

slides.text: Vikram didn't call directly. He sent an associate. 'FlashBasket wants to explore a strategic partnership with StockSense.' Priya Googled FlashBasket's recent numbers. Then she called Vikram directly. 'Let's skip the associate. I know what you want.'

Same Bandra hotel where Arjun signed the territory deal. Priya sat in the same chair. She'd done her homework. 'Your integration failed. Your stores are bleeding. You need my inventory AI. What's your offer?'
Vikram offered ₹15 crore for StockSense. Classic lowball. Priya laughed. 'I'm not selling. I'm licensing. ₹2 crore per year. Plus I get access to your dark store data. You don't buy me. You rent me.'

Why did Priya want FlashBasket's data? Not for FlashBasket. For StockSense. 180 dark stores worth of inventory data would make her AI the most powerful in Indian retail. She was using the predator to feed her own system.

Vikram agreed. He had no choice. Within 6 months, StockSense's AI reduced FlashBasket's inventory waste by 40%. It worked. Beautifully. Which meant Vikram owed his survival to the co-founder of the company he killed.

episodes.synopsis: Vikram reaches out to Priya. He wants her tech. She wants something else entirely.
episodes.caption: The co-founder who was pushed out saved the competitor who killed her company. Not out of kindness. Out of strategy. She used the predator to build the biggest inventory AI in India. The math always wins. 📞

episodes.title: The Room

slides.text: BizIndia Summit 2027. India's biggest startup conference. Vikram was a speaker. Arjun was in the audience. Priya was backstage. Neha was moderating a panel. The first time all four were in the same building since the crash.
Neha's panel topic: 'When Startups Die — What We Learn.' She invited Arjun on stage. He hesitated. Then walked up. The audience went quiet. The guy from that LinkedIn post was here. In person.

Arjun spoke for 12 minutes. No slides. No script. He listed every mistake. The changed model. The ignored CFO. The unread clause. The bad hire. 'I was the biggest risk in my own company. Not the market. Not the competition. Me.'

After the panel, Priya found Arjun backstage. 'StockSense needs a sales head. Someone who can talk to founders. Someone who's been through it. Interested?' He stared. 'You'd hire me? After everything?' 'BECAUSE of everything.'

Arjun joined StockSense. Not as a co-founder. As an employee. First day — he sat at a regular desk. No glass office. No Forbes frame. Just a laptop and a framed printout of Neha's rule: 'Change the model, not the math.'

episodes.synopsis: One year after QuickKart's death. A startup conference in Mumbai. All the players in one room. An unexpected pitch.
episodes.caption: The founder who lost ₹100 crore. Working as employee number 13. At the company built by the co-founder he pushed out. Sometimes the best second act starts at a regular desk. 🪑

episodes.title: The Spreadsheet

slides.text: ₹100 crore. Sounds like infinite money until you have 400 people, 47 dark stores, and a VP who thinks Goa offsites are 'team building.' Here's where every rupee went.

Salaries & HR: ₹22 Cr. Dark stores (rent, setup): ₹28 Cr. Marketing & brand: ₹18 Cr. Delivery subsidies: ₹12 Cr. Tech & infrastructure: ₹8 Cr. Legal & compliance: ₹2 Cr. 'Miscellaneous': ₹10 Cr. Total: ₹100 Cr. Time: 18 months.

Of the ₹18 Cr marketing spend: ₹7 Cr on influencers (ROI: 0.3%). ₹5 Cr on cricket sponsorship (no measurable orders). ₹3 Cr on a Bollywood brand deal (actor posted once, forgot to tag them). ₹3 Cr on performance ads (the only thing that worked).

The ₹10 Cr 'miscellaneous': Goa offsite ₹1.2 Cr. Founder's apartment (called 'office space'): ₹48L. International 'research trips': ₹85L. 'Consultant fees' to friends of the VP: ₹3.2 Cr. The rest? Genuinely unaccounted.

₹100 crore. If spent at ₹3 Cr/month (lean burn), QuickKart had 33 months of runway. Instead, they burned at ₹12 Cr/month and died in 8. The difference between surviving and dying was a spreadsheet nobody respected.

episodes.synopsis: A forensic breakdown of where ₹100 crore actually went. Numbers don't lie.
episodes.caption: ₹100 crore broken down to the last rupee. Goa offsites as team building. An apartment as office space. ₹4 crore that simply vanished. If you had ₹100 Cr and 33 months, what would you build? 📊

episodes.title: The Investors

slides.text: NexGen Capital manages ₹800 crore. They need to deploy it all within 3 years. If they don't invest fast enough, their OWN investors pull money. So they invest in quantity. Not quality. QuickKart was investment #47.
VC math: invest in 50 companies, hope 3 become huge. The other 47? Expected to fail. QuickKart wasn't special. It was a lottery ticket. And nobody cries over a losing lottery ticket.

SilkRoute's partner, Meghna, pushed for aggressive growth because SilkRoute needed a quick win for their annual report. Not for QuickKart's benefit. For their next fundraise. The startup was a data point in someone else's pitch deck.

VCs raise from LPs. LPs want 3x returns. VCs need fast exits. Fast exits need fast growth. Fast growth needs aggressive spending. Aggressive spending kills startups. Dead startups become write-offs. VCs raise the next fund. The cycle continues.
QuickKart wasn't killed by one bad decision. It was killed by a system designed to create fast-growth, cash-burning companies. Arjun was the founder. But the system was the co-founder nobody blames.

episodes.synopsis: The investor side. NexGen and SilkRoute had their own pressures. The system that creates bad startups.
episodes.caption: VCs invest to deploy capital, not to build companies. Fast growth isn't a strategy — it's a requirement of the system. QuickKart was designed to burn. The system demands it. Is the system broken or working as intended? ⚙️

episodes.title: The WhatsApp Group

slides.text: Rahul — rider #47. When QuickKart shut down, he had ₹2,300 in his account and a ₹4,700 bike EMI due in 6 days. He created a WhatsApp group: 'QuickKart Riders — Now What?' 53 people joined in an hour.
They wrote a letter to QuickKart's management. 178 signatures. Demanding: 3 months' notice pay, EMI support, and an apology. The letter was returned. 'QuickKart no longer operates at this address.'

Rahul had an idea. They couldn't fight in court — no money for lawyers. But they had something better. 178 people who knew every dark store location, every supplier, every delivery route. They had information. And a journalist cousin.

The Print published: 'QuickKart's Ghost Workers: 178 Riders Left With No Pay, No Notice, and Bike EMIs They Can't Escape.' It went viral. 2 lakh shares. Suddenly, everyone cared about the riders. When the headline was right.

FlashBasket — who bought QuickKart's assets — offered to hire 120 of the 178 riders. Not charity. Smart PR. Arjun, through Neha's firm, set up an EMI relief fund. ₹18 lakhs. Small. But real. More than the company ever gave them.

episodes.synopsis: The 178 delivery riders who got nothing. Their WhatsApp group becomes a movement.
episodes.caption: 178 riders. One WhatsApp group. A journalist cousin. Sometimes the most powerful people in a startup story aren't the founders or investors. They're the people who did the actual work. 📱

episodes.title: The 10 Rules

slides.text: Rule 1: If your CFO writes a report, READ IT. Neha's 12-page analysis predicted the crash 8 months early. Nobody read it. Rule 2: Never change the model to fit the pitch. Change the pitch to fit the model.

Rule 3: Read page 47. Every contract has a kill clause hidden somewhere. Find it before you sign. Rule 4: Check references. ₹85 lakh salary and not one phone call to verify Rohit's claims. One call could have saved ₹18 crore.

Rule 5: A co-founder who disagrees with you is worth more than one who agrees. Priya was right about 30-minute delivery. Arjun fired his best advisor. Rule 6: Revenue is vanity. Cash is reality. ₹8 Cr revenue meant nothing with ₹14 Cr costs.

Rule 7: Mandatory spend clauses exist to benefit investors, not you. If someone forces you to spend, ask why. Rule 8: Your delivery riders are your company. Not your pitch deck. Not your valuation. The 178 people doing the actual work.

Rule 9: The competitor offering a 'friendly deal' is never friendly. Every deal has a winner. Make sure it's you. Rule 10: If you fail — fail publicly. Arjun's conference speech created more value than his ₹100 Cr ever did.

episodes.synopsis: The lessons from QuickKart's crash, distilled into 10 rules for every startup founder.
episodes.caption: 10 rules from a ₹100 crore crash. Which one would have saved YOUR startup? Save this for every founder you know. 📌

slides.text: Arjun is StockSense's head of sales. Salary: ₹22 lakhs/year. He paid off his personal guarantee. He hasn't opened the Forbes article once. His LinkedIn bio says: 'I help founders avoid my mistakes.'
StockSense hit 15,000 stores. Revenue: ₹9 crore. She took her first investor — a single angel for ₹2 crore at a fair valuation. No ratchets. No mandatory spend. No page 47. The terms fit on one page.

Neha's consulting firm has 40 startup clients. She makes every founder sign one thing before she takes them on: 'I will not change the model to fit the pitch.' Three have refused. All three are already shutting down.
FlashBasket merged with a bigger player — ZipMart. Vikram got a payout and a board seat. He's fine. He'll always be fine. The system protects its architects.

₹100 crore destroyed one company and rebuilt three careers. The money is gone. The lessons aren't. Somewhere in Mumbai right now, a founder is editing their financial model. Changing the numbers to look better. The cycle is restarting.

episodes.synopsis: Two years after the crash. Everyone's different. The startup ecosystem moved on. But did it learn?
episodes.caption: The story ends. The cycle doesn't. Somewhere right now, someone is making the same choices Arjun did. Will they read this series in time? Tag a founder who needs to see this. 🔁

episodes.title: Neha

slides.text: Neha Agarwal. CA at 23. Worked at Deloitte for 3 years. Left because she wanted to build, not audit. Joined QuickKart as employee #7. She was the first person who wasn't a friend of Arjun or Priya.

She wrote 14 financial reports in 18 months. Arjun read the first 3. Skimmed the next 4. Ignored the rest. Each report got more urgent. The last one's subject line: 'READ THIS OR I RESIGN.' He read it. Then promoted her to CFO. And ignored the report.

'Why didn't you leave earlier?' everyone asks. Her answer: 'Because 400 people relied on those paychecks. If I left, there'd be nobody watching the money. Nobody sounding the alarm. I stayed for them, not for Arjun.'

The day QuickKart shut down, Neha didn't go home. She stayed to process final salaries. ₹1.8 crore — the last money in the account. She made sure every employee got their last month. Arjun found out after. He hadn't even thought of it.

Today, every startup Neha consults for has a non-negotiable: the CFO reports to the board, not the CEO. She built a system where the person watching the money can't be silenced. It took ₹100 crore to learn that. But now it's law.

episodes.synopsis: The CFO who warned everyone. Her backstory and why she stayed as long as she did.
episodes.caption: She wrote 14 warnings. Was ignored 14 times. Stayed to protect 400 paychecks. Processed the final salaries when nobody else remembered. The real hero isn't always the founder. 📝

episodes.title: The Speech

slides.text: BizIndia Summit 2028. Arjun got a proper speaker invite this time. Topic: 'Why Your Startup Will Die — A Mathematical Certainty.' Sold out. The audience wanted blood. He gave them a mirror.

He showed 50 startup pitch decks (anonymized). Then their actual results 2 years later. 43 of 50 had changed their financial models to look better. 41 of those 43 were now dead or dying. 'The correlation is 95%. The model editing kills.'

He looked at Vikram. 'Predatory term sheets don't fail because they're predatory. They fail because they force the same burn-and-die pattern. You're not building companies. You're building funeral pyres with ₹100 crore of someone else's money.'

Standing ovation. 800 people. Vikram stayed seated. A young founder in the back row started crying — she'd just signed a term sheet with a ratchet clause that morning. She called her lawyer from the hallway.
Arjun ended with: 'I'm not here because I succeeded. I'm here because I survived. And the difference is ₹100 crore and four hundred people's lives. Don't let that be your tuition fee too.'

episodes.synopsis: One year after the BizIndia Summit, Arjun speaks again. This time, he has data. And an audience that includes Vikram.
episodes.caption: 800 people standing. One founder calling her lawyer to undo a bad deal. If one speech saves one company — the ₹100 crore wasn't wasted. It was tuition. 🎤

episodes.title: The Rohit Problem

slides.text: Six months after QuickKart died, Rohit updated his LinkedIn. 'VP of Growth, QuickKart (Grew MAU 300% in 6 months).' He didn't mention the crash. Or the burn. Or the ₹18 crore. LinkedIn only shows the highlight reel.

He got hired at another startup. VP of Marketing. ₹92 lakhs. Nobody called QuickKart for a reference. Nobody checked the real numbers. The same resume. A different company. The same playbook about to repeat.

In 18 months, the new startup shut down too. Rohit's third company in 5 years. All dead. His salary total across three startups: ₹2.1 crore. Value destroyed: estimated ₹45 crore. He's interviewing again. This week.

The Rohit problem: startups hire for brand names, not results. Nobody calls references. Nobody asks 'what happened AFTER you grew 300%?' The ecosystem has no immune system against professional destroyers.

Neha's firm now offers 'Hire Check' — a service where they audit senior hire claims against actual company data. First finding: 60% of VP-level candidates inflated their impact by 2-5x. The Rohit problem has a solution. Nobody's buying it yet.

episodes.synopsis: What happened to Rohit — the VP of Growth who burned ₹18 crore. He's fine. And that's the problem.
episodes.caption: He burned ₹18 crore at QuickKart. Got hired at a higher salary. Burned another company. Interviewing again. The startup ecosystem's biggest vulnerability isn't bad ideas. It's failing to check who you're hiring. 🔍

episodes.title: The Ecosystem

slides.text: In 2025, India had 1.12 lakh registered startups. 90% will fail within 5 years. That's not a statistic. That's over 1 lakh founders who'll experience what Arjun did. Some will learn. Most won't get the chance.

The cycle: Idea → Hype → Raise → Burn → Pivot → Raise Again → Burn Again → Die → LinkedIn Post. Repeat x 1 lakh. The ecosystem doesn't learn because the people who profit from the cycle don't need it to change.

But something's changing. Bootstrapped companies like StockSense are proving profitability isn't boring — it's survivable. Revenue-first isn't slow. It's sustainable. And a new generation of founders is choosing boring math over exciting hype.

₹100 crore could fund 100 bootstrapped startups at ₹1 crore each. Or 10 sustainable companies at ₹10 crore. Instead it funded one company that burned everything in 6 months. The allocation is the problem.

This series isn't anti-startup. It's anti-stupidity. Build things. Raise money. Grow fast if you can. But read the report. Check the reference. Read page 47. And if the math doesn't work — change the model, not the math.

episodes.synopsis: A wide-angle look at India's startup ecosystem and what QuickKart's story means for everyone in it.
episodes.caption: 24 episodes. One crash. Infinite lessons. The math doesn't lie. The models can be fixed. The ecosystem can change. But only if founders stop changing the numbers and start changing the game. 🎯

episodes.title: The Timeline

slides.text: MAY 2023: Juhu beach. The idea. JUNE-NOV 2023: Build and launch. First delivery: 9 min 12 sec. JAN 2024: Priya leaves. The last voice of reason exits.
APR 2024: The flaw is buried. The model changes. OCT 2024: ₹100 Cr raised. The treadmill starts. FEB 2025: Rohit hired. The burn accelerates. APR 2025: The deal with FlashBasket. Page 47 unread.

JUL 2025: Best month. Worst economics. Neha's report ignored for the last time. OCT 2025: MAU drops below danger line. NOV 2025: Cash runs out. DEC 2025: Panic. Desperation fundraise fails. JAN 2026: Dead.

400 jobs lost. 178 riders unpaid. ₹100 Cr gone. But: Neha's consulting firm protects 40 companies. Priya's StockSense serves 15,000 stores. Arjun helps founders avoid his path. Rahul still rides. The story isn't just death. It's also what grows after.

Every episode asked: what would you have done differently? Now you know the whole story. The beach. The lie. The deal. The crash. The aftermath. The question isn't what went wrong. It's: are you making the same choices right now?

episodes.synopsis: The complete chronological timeline of QuickKart — from beach to crash. Every decision, every missed signal, mapped.
episodes.caption: 25 episodes. From crash to origin to aftermath. Every mistake was a choice. Every choice was avoidable. If this series saved you one bad decision — it was worth more than ₹100 crore ever was. Share this with every founder you know. 🏁
